title: Knowledge Check 10: Lessons 73-81
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 73-81 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: An architect is routing one inbound Case to different assignment queues based on its priority, then plans to enrich the record with account data from a separate API call. Per the lesson's shapes, which two named patterns does this design use, and which property must the routing step respect?
options: A Message Router for the priority-based routing and a Content Enricher for the account lookup, with the router directed not to modify the message contents.
An Aggregator for the priority-based routing and a Content Filter for the account lookup, with the aggregator directed to modify the message contents.
A Content-Based Router combined with a Splitter, with the router allowed to reshape the message as it decides the destination.
A Resequencer for the routing and a Canonical Data Model for the enricher, with the enricher allowed to drop the priority field.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the Message Router as a filter that decides a message's destination without modifying the message contents, and the Content Enricher as the transformation that adds data a sender did not provide. The routing step must never also reshape the message, which is the router discipline the lesson emphasizes.

questions.question: An ERP requires XML while Salesforce uses JSON, and a review asks why the integration defines one internal canonical Customer contract instead of mapping each pair of systems directly. Which reasoning does the lesson give?
options: A canonical model converts N-times-M source-to-target mappings into N plus M, which is why it makes the translator family maintainable as more systems join.
A canonical model removes the need for any translators because every system adopts the same binary payload over the wire.
A canonical model only helps when there are exactly two systems, so it is the wrong choice for a many-system integration.
A canonical model is required by External Services and cannot be built in Apex.
questions.explanation: The lesson says translating every source to every target is N-times-M translations, while translating each source to one canonical model and each target from it is N plus M, and it calls the Canonical Data Model the translator family's organizing principle that keeps integrations maintainable as systems join.

questions.question: A quoting service fans a request out to three banks and must return the best rate, but speed matters more than waiting for every response. Which completeness condition does the lesson direct this design to use, and why?
options: First best, which waits for the first response and ignores the rest, practical in a bidding or quoting scenario where response time is critical.
Wait for all, which never publishes until every bank has answered, guaranteeing the best possible rate.
External event, which waits for the end of a trading day before combining any responses.
A fixed count of zero, so the aggregator publishes an empty combined result immediately.
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the aggregator completeness strategies and describes first best as waiting only for the first fastest response and ignoring the others, calling it practical in a bidding or quoting scenario where response time is critical, which matches the quote use case.

questions.question: A team splits its application into many independently deployable services, but every service still connects directly to every partner system with no mediator. Per the lesson, what has the team actually decided?
options: It has chosen microservices on the code-splitting axis but has not chosen a hub on the topology axis, so the point-to-point wiring problem remains unsolved.
It has fully adopted a hub-and-spoke topology because the services are independently deployable.
It has eliminated the need for a system of record because each service owns its own data.
It has made Salesforce the integration hub by virtue of splitting the code into services.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates two independent axes: how many deployable units the code splits into (monolith vs microservices) and which systems connect directly vs through a mediating hub (topology). Splitting into services does not create a hub; the point-to-point wiring problem from Lesson 8 remains unless something mediates.

questions.question: A company's official customer master lives in an on-prem ERP, and Salesforce holds a synced copy for the sales team. A consultant proposes making Salesforce the integration hub. What does the lesson say is the honest first step?
options: Name Salesforce as the spoke it currently is, or design explicitly to move the system of record, because hub status follows from where the authoritative copy actually lives.
Centralize all traffic in Salesforce immediately, since a synced copy is close enough to the source of truth.
Split the ERP into microservices so that Salesforce can become the hub without moving any data.
Reject the proposal outright, because Salesforce can never be a hub when any other system exists.
questions.explanation: The lesson's system-of-record test says the hub is the owner of the authoritative entity. If the ERP holds the official customer master and Salesforce holds a copy, Salesforce is a spoke. A hub proposal must either move the system of record or be honest that it is converging at a copy that can drift.

questions.question: A hub fans a confirmed order out to the ERP and the billing platform, and the ERP's fulfillment endpoint answers in ten seconds. Per the lesson, what is the correct design response?
options: Keep the call synchronous on the rep's request path, because a ten-second callout is within the synchronous budget.
Move the fan-out onto a platform event and let a Queueable or Flow drive it with a timeout and retry policy matched to the ERP, returning the page immediately with a processing state.
Increase the per-transaction SOQL and DML limits so the synchronous callout has more headroom.
Route the call through a bespoke microservices layer so the platform's governor limits no longer apply.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a ten-second user-facing callout against the synchronous budget is the wrong shape. The fix is to move the fan-out onto a platform event and let an asynchronous consumer drive it with a timeout and retry policy, returning the page immediately with a processing state, per the reliability guidance on operation-appropriate timeouts.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the single load-bearing difference between a workflow and an agent?
options: A workflow is fixed code paths orchestrating LLMs and tools, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool usage.
A workflow uses many models while an agent uses one model.
A workflow never calls tools while an agent always does.
A workflow runs on a server while an agent runs on a client device.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's distinction is that a workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes the task.

questions.question: A team is building an agent that needs to research a service failure that could have several independent root causes. The plan-and-execute approach is chosen. What best describes what happens when one executor returns an unexpected result?
options: The system immediately stops and returns an error to the user.
The planner is called again with a re-planning prompt to decide whether to finish or generate a follow-up plan.
Every executor re-runs its tool calls from scratch in a new context window.
The orchestration moves from a single agent to a workflow with fixed code paths.
questions.explanation: In plan-and-execute, once execution completes, the agent is called again with a re-planning prompt that lets it decide whether to finish with a response or generate a follow-up plan when the first plan did not have the desired effect.

questions.question: A client asks to scale its research agent into a multi-agent orchestrator-worker system. Using the lesson's token accounting, what should the architect weigh before committing?
options: Multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats, so the added capability must earn the increased spend.
Single-agent systems always use more tokens than multi-agent systems.
Tokens are the same regardless of the number of agents.
Multi-agent systems reduce token use because subagents share one context window.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's data shows agents use about 4x more tokens than chat while multi-agent systems use about 15x more than chats, so multi-agent architectures require tasks with high enough value to pay for the increased performance.

questions.question: An Enterprise Edition org has 120 Salesforce licenses, 30 Salesforce Platform licenses, and 800 Customer Community Plus licenses, with no API add-ons. What is the org's daily API request allocation?
options: 150,000 calls
310,000 calls
250,000 calls
390,000 calls
questions.explanation: The Enterprise Edition formula is 100,000 base plus licenses times the per-license rate. That gives 100,000 + (120 x 1,000) + (30 x 1,000) + (800 x 200) = 100,000 + 120,000 + 30,000 + 160,000 = 310,000 calls per 24 hours.

questions.question: A nightly integration must upsert 250,000 product records into Salesforce. A developer proposes one REST call per record. Using the lesson's reasoning, what is the correct design and why?
options: Keep the per-record REST design, because the daily request allocation is large enough to absorb 250,000 calls.
Move the load to Bulk API 2.0, because any operation over roughly 2,000 records belongs there and its ingest batches draw from the separate 15,000-batch pool rather than the daily request allocation.
Keep the per-record design but schedule it during business hours so it is metered against interactive user traffic.
Move the load to Platform Events, because event publishes do not count toward any allocation.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that any operation over about 2,000 records belongs in Bulk API 2.0, and that Bulk API has its own separate allocation of 15,000 batches per rolling 24 hours shared with Bulk API, with ingest jobs consuming batches. The cost unit is the call, not the record, so per-record REST turns a modest bulk job into hundreds of thousands of calls.

questions.question: A service agent runs 30,000 conversations a month at four standard actions each in production. Its prompt context carries 6,500 tokens per turn. Using the August 2026 rate card, which statement correctly describes the consumption?
options: Actions cost 120,000 credits and each turn bills one prompt unit, because prompts are billed per request regardless of size.
Actions cost 2.4 million credits, and each turn bills four prompt units because billing rounds up in 2,000-token blocks; trimming context under 2,000 tokens would cut that to one unit per turn.
Actions cost 2.4 million credits, and each turn bills one prompt unit because only input tokens are counted.
Actions cost 600,000 credits, and each turn bills three prompt units because the rate card caps prompts at 6,000 tokens.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the Standard Action multiplier as 20 in production, so 30,000 conversations x 4 actions = 120,000 actions x 20 = 2.4 million credits. Prompt billing works in blocks of up to 2,000 tokens rounded up, and the lesson's example shows 6,500 tokens metering as four units, while anything under 2,000 tokens bills one unit.

questions.question: An org has a daily API allocation of 500,000 calls. Peak-day consumption is 325,000 and has grown 10 percent per quarter. Using the lesson's runway formula, which statement is correct?
options: Headroom is 35 percent, and runway is about 4.6 quarters, so roughly fourteen months.
Headroom is 35 percent, and runway is about 9 quarters, because growth of 10 percent per quarter takes 90 percent of the remaining time to reach the limit.
Headroom is 65 percent, and runway is about 2 quarters because the peak is already close to the limit.
Headroom is 35 percent, and runway cannot be computed without knowing the average consumption over the same period.
questions.explanation: Headroom is (500,000 - 325,000) / 500,000 = 35 percent. Runway is ln(500,000 / 325,000) / ln(1.10) = 0.4318 / 0.0953 = about 4.5 quarters, roughly fourteen months. The lesson shows this same calculation at 280,000 and 196,000.

questions.question: The service console's default list view filters a 12 million row Case object on Status != 'Closed', and it has slowed from two seconds to twenty. A stakeholder asks for more CPU capacity. What does the lesson say to do first?
options: Buy more capacity, because a scan on 12 million rows is a platform limit and cannot be fixed by design.

Fix the design first: the negation filter on a low-cardinality field causes a scan, so filter on a selective indexed value such as an IsClosed boolean, add a custom index, and decompose the query if multiple WHERE filters block index use.
Move the list view to a scheduled report, because list views are not indexable.
Convert the object to a Big Object so performance stays consistent at any volume.
questions.explanation: The lesson's decision rule puts the waste question first. The tuning guidance it cites says null and non-selective filters do not use the index, and in some cases multiple WHERE filters prevent index use, in which case you decompose into narrower queries. Buying capacity does not make a full-table scan faster.

questions.question: A monthly load of 400,000 records runs as one REST call per record against an allocation of 280,000 calls per day, and a developer says the sandbox test finished in 40 minutes so it is fine. What is the correct reading?
options: The test proves capacity is sufficient, because 40 minutes is well inside the nightly window.

The load alone exceeds the daily allocation at 400,000 calls, so callers fail and retries make it worse. It should move to Bulk API 2.0, whose batches draw from a separate allocation pool, and the sandbox result only proved data volume behavior, not production concurrency.
The load is acceptable because REST calls are not counted against the API allocation when they run outside business hours.
The load is acceptable if the developer raises the batch size in the REST request payload.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the cost unit is the call, not the record, so 400,000 records as individual REST calls consumes 400,000 calls against a 280,000 daily allocation. It also states that a full copy sandbox proves data-volume behavior and not concurrency, so a comfortable sandbox timing is a floor rather than a prediction.

questions.question: A release manager has 90 change requests for the quarter and 13 production windows that each handle 4 changes. The team responds by bundling unrelated work into single change sets and by declaring more requests urgent. Per the lesson, what is the actual defect and the correct first move?
options: The team is not working enough weekends. Add a second Saturday window and require overtime sign-off.
Validation and deployment are too slow. Automate them and the 38-change shortfall closes.
Two risk classes are sharing one pipe. Classify the low-risk reports and permission work into a separate, more frequent lane so the heavy window is no longer overloaded.
The intake queue is the problem. Ask the business to submit fewer requests until the backlog clears.
questions.explanation: Fifty-two slots against 90 requests leaves 38 changes unshippable per quarter. The lesson's worked example shows the shortfall closes when standard-tier work moves to a weekly lane, leaving 30 heavy changes across 13 windows against a capacity of 4. Faster validation does not fix a constraint that is window frequency and classification.

questions.question: An architect is defending a production change policy that says any failed release will be rolled back to the previous state. The team deploys with change sets. What must the architect change about that promise?
options: Nothing. A failed change set deployment rolls back the whole transaction automatically.

A successful change set deployment cannot be rolled back and change sets cannot delete or rename components, so recovery means a forward fix or a separately deployed previous metadata state, and the review gate has to carry more weight.
Change sets can be recalled after upload, so rollback is available as long as the architect acts within the same day.
Rollback is available only when the target is a sandbox, so production policy should reference the sandbox procedure.
questions.explanation: Change set deployment is a one-way transaction: if it fails partway the transaction rolls back, but once it succeeds the changes are committed. Combined with the inability to delete or rename components and the ban on recalling an uploaded change set, the policy has to be rewritten around validation and forward repair.

questions.question: Emergency changes are 28 percent of a client's production changes, and the CAB responds by requiring more approvals on the emergency path. Why does the lesson call that the wrong fix?
options: Emergency volume is unrelated to process design and should be tracked only for audit purposes.
A high emergency share means the normal path is too slow or unpredictable, so tightening the emergency path leaves the cause in place and pushes teams to bypass governance another way.
Emergencies should be blocked entirely, because production defects never justify an unplanned change.
The right fix is to remove the emergency tier and route every change through the major tier for consistency.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats emergency inflation as a process defect: teams declare emergencies because waiting on the normal path costs more. The fix is to measure normal lead time, find the waiting, and shorten the normal path, not to add friction to the only route that currently works.

questions.question: An architect discovers that an accepted ADR's decision no longer applies because the ERP vendor changed its API rate limits. According to the lesson, what is the correct way to handle the record?
options: Edit the accepted ADR in place so it reflects the new vendor terms and current practice.
Delete the record and replace it with an updated design document section.
Write a new ADR that supersedes it, change the old record's status to Superseded, and point to the replacement.
Change the old record's status back to Proposed so the team can debate it again.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that an accepted ADR is immutable. When circumstances change, the team writes a new record that supersedes the old one, and the old record stays in place with its status changed to Superseded and a pointer to its replacement. Editing it in place destroys the historical integrity of the log, and deleting it removes the record of what the team believed at the time.

questions.question: A program's architecture meeting notes contain 31 decisions from one quarter, but only 9 of them appear in the decision log. Using the lesson's decision debt arithmetic, what does this ratio indicate and what is the recommended fix?
options: About 71 percent of decisions are invisible; require the record before the decision is final and enforce a merge gate that asks for the ADR number.
About 29 percent of decisions are documented, which is acceptable; add a quarterly summary document to close the gap.
About 9 percent of decisions are at risk; assign a technical writer to transcribe the meeting notes after each session.
About 71 percent of decisions are invisible; the correct fix is to reduce the number of decisions made each quarter.
questions.explanation: The lesson computes decision debt as recorded decisions divided by total decisions. Nine of 31 leaves 22 invisible, which is about 71 percent. The fix it recommends is mechanical: require the record before the decision becomes final, while alternatives are still live, and enforce a merge gate that asks for the ADR number on architecturally significant changes. Transcription after the fact is the ADR theater failure mode.

questions.question: In the order-to-inventory worked example, a direct callout design would produce 80,000 API calls against a 100,000 daily allocation at peak. Which consequence argument from the lesson best supports choosing Platform Events instead?
options: Platform Events are always less expensive than API callouts, so the cost saving alone justifies the decision.
Consuming 80 percent of the allocation leaves only 20,000 calls for retries, backfills, and every other integration, so one retry storm can fail unrelated work.
A nightly batch is the only design that prevents inventory oversell, so events are chosen to replace the batch.
The daily API limit resets every 24 hours, so using 80 percent at peak has no effect on other integrations.
questions.explanation: The lesson's arithmetic shows 40,000 orders times two calls equals 80,000, or 80 percent of a 100,000 daily allocation. The remaining 20,000 calls must absorb retries, backfills, support tooling, marketing sync, and every other integration, which creates a shared failure mode. The ADR chooses events for decoupling and near real time behavior while accepting eventual consistency, not because events are inherently cheaper. The lesson rejects the nightly batch because it allows up to 24 hours of inventory staleness.

questions.question: A team documents every model in its support agent, one card per model, and considers the system documented. Per the lesson, what is missing from that set?
options: Nothing important, because a model card already reports intended use and disaggregated evaluation results.
The router, retrieval, tools, prompts, and permissions, which decide behavior but appear in no model card.
The training dataset, which a model card covers for vendor models but not for fine-tuned ones.
The vendor's release notes, which replace the need for an organizational evaluation section.
questions.explanation: A system is not a model. Routing between models, retrieval sources, exposed actions, and guardrail configuration are system-level facts, which is why the system card exists.

questions.question: An architect drafts a system card for an Agentforce service agent that states sensitive data is masked before prompts reach the model. What does the lesson say about that statement?
options: It is accurate as long as Data Cloud is provisioned, because the Trust Layer depends on Data Cloud.
It is accurate because masking is enabled by default and covers all generative AI surfaces in the org.
It restates a platform capability that does not apply here, since data masking for LLMs is disabled for agents.
It is accurate only if the agent uses the console channel rather than Experience Cloud.
questions.explanation: The Trust Layer setup documentation states that data masking for LLMs is disabled for agents. A system card records configured behavior, so the control has to be checked for the specific surface, not copied from the platform capability list.

questions.question: An architect compares the live org configuration (model snapshot, active prompt template version, action list, Trust Layer settings) against what the system card claims. Which outcome does the lesson identify as the one that produces incidents?
options: The card is stale because the team stopped updating it after launch.
The configuration was changed by someone who did not know the card existed.
The evaluation report predates the current golden set version.
The card lists a control that is a platform default rather than a configured setting.
questions.explanation: A stale card is a maintenance problem, but an undocumented configuration change means the running system is unknown to the people accountable for it, which is the failure the quarterly diff is designed to catch.

questions.question: A candidate writes decision 4 in the scenario document: Salesforce owns the commercial shipment record and the transportation management system owns milestone events. The decision appears on the system map. Asked what the choice costs, the candidate says it costs nothing because both systems keep their existing roles. Applying the lesson's completeness test, what is the problem?
options: The decision is invalid because two systems cannot both hold shipment-related data.
The area is complete, since a decision with no cost means the choice was genuinely free.
The area is not complete: the test needs a decision, a carrier and a stated tradeoff, and a claim of zero cost usually means the cost has not been found yet.
The candidate should remove the decision from the diagram so judges cannot question it.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the completeness test as three legs: a decision, the artifact that carries it, and the tradeoff accepted. The candidate has the first two. Saying the choice costs nothing usually means the cost is unexamined, and in this example the read-model split carries real costs in freshness and operational overhead. If a decision has no cost, the thinking is not finished.

questions.question: It is minute 130 of the 180-minute preparation. The candidate has a system map, a data model, a security model and an NFR table, but the slide deck is empty and the traceability matrix is missing rows for six secondary requirements. Which move matches the lesson's triage order?
options: Finish the six traceability rows first, then build the slides as quickly as possible.
Build the slide deck now and record the six secondary requirement rows as named gaps.
Redraw the system map with cleaner notation so the slides are faster to assemble.
Skip the consistency pass to recover the time spent on the missing rows.
questions.explanation: The lesson's cut-first list includes secondary requirements and visual polish, while the deck and the consistency pass sit in the protect-last group because the deck is the only artifact judges see during the presentation and the consistency pass catches contradictions between artifacts. Named gaps are respected; unmentioned omissions are not.

questions.question: During the 45-minute presentation, a candidate plans to show three viable architecture options and let the judges discuss which one they prefer. What does the lesson say about that approach?
options: It is correct, because letting the board choose shows collaboration and openness.
It is correct as long as each option is described in the same amount of detail.
It is a mistake: present a recommendation and frame the other options as rejected alternatives, since options without a recommendation are sloppy advisory.
It is a mistake only if the judges ask for a recommendation during the questions.
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes Salesforce's stakeholder guidance directly: providing options without recommendations is sloppy advisory. The presentation should lead with a recommendation and treat the alternatives as rejected choices with reasons, so judges spend their time testing whether the details support the recommendation.
